subject: between-group comparisons of effect size in compare.pls()

messages.author: 06c72fc2e70ccfe4
messages.subject: between-group comparisons of effect size in compare.pls()
parts:
Hi all,

I am working with morphometric data from 12 populations of stickleback from 6 watersheds, each with a lake and a stream population.  I am interested in comparing integration of two blocks of data between populations, but also the effects of habitat (lake or stream) and watershed on integration of the two blocks.  I have run integration.test and compare.pls, which worked nicely for comparisons between populations, but I am struggling a bit with how to test for habitat and watershed effects.

I was hoping to use aovSufficient in the HH package to run a habitat*watershed ANOVA using the population Z-scores and SDs yielded by compare.pls, but considering the pairwise comparisons in the compare.pls output are so conservative relative to the results aovSufficient is providing, I am wondering whether I have misunderstood something about the SDs yielded by compare.pls's resampling procedure.  The pairwise effect sizes and p-values yielded by compare.pls (in attachment) also seem quite conservative when the within population Z-scores ± SDs are plotted:

Is this ANOVA an appropriate way to conduct this comparison, and if not, is there an alternative method I could use to test habitat*population effects on integration?


thanks very much,


Grant Haines

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] between-group comparisons of effect size in compare.pls()
parts:
Grant,

I’m not sure what the functions in the HH package do (appears they are companion functions for a statistics text) but it appears you misinterpreted some of the output from a compare.pls object when using those functions.  It appears you used the $sample.z output as points in your plot and the $sample.r.sd as error bars.  The SD values are not for the z-scores; they are for the r-pls values of the PLS analysis.  If you plot each sample's r-pls with these SD values as error bars, the analyses would not appear so conservative.

The z-scores are calculated from r-pls and the SD of r-pls as z =  (r.pls - mean)/SD, where mean is the mean of r-pls across the PLS permutations.  This is a summary statistic, not an estimate with a standard error.  There is no reason to plot z-scores and error bars.  Judging by your sample z-scores, which tend to be small, it is no surprise that the pairwise z-scores are also small.  If you do not have much integration in your samples, as a start, then it is unlikely, if not impossible, that you have large differences in integration between samples.  I think you were mislead by plotting standard deviations as error bars for the wrong statistics.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] between-group comparisons of effect size in compare.pls()
parts:
Grant,

 

To add to Mike’s cogent comment, it sounds like your intention is to use output of integration to ask a subsequent question regarding groups. Statistically, such analyses fall into meta-analysis: ‘statistics summarizing prior statistical results.’ Quantitative meta-analyses have been a standard part of the statistical toolkit in psychometrics for 40 years (since Glass’ seminal 1976 paper), and has been widely utilized in some areas of biostatistics for several decades also.

 

One could, in fact, consider our Z-score test to compare pairs of integration levels in this manner. However, analyses of this sort for integration for ‘higher’ level designs (e.g., your factorial model), have not been considered analytically. That would take some work to verify that the individual integration Z-scores are appropriate for that application.

 

Dean
